section_summary: This section traces Japanese commercial travel, suspected intelligence networks, espionage reports, and propaganda activity across the Americas from August 1941 through January 1942. It includes FBI and military-intelligence reports, travel lists, cross-reference sheets, a Coordinator of Information survey of possible agents, intercepted coded-message traffic immediately after Pearl Harbor, and reports of possible sabotage preparations. The final portion consists chiefly of diplomatic replies assessing the extent and effect of Japanese propaganda in individual Latin American and Caribbean countries.

subfiles.title: FBI report on a Japanese commercial conference at São Paulo
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Takeo Nishizawa's trip to a conference on Japanese inter-American trade and Itaro Amari's concern about a prospective American blacklist.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source said representatives from every South American country met at Casa Tozan in São Paulo to plan trade in the event of war in Asia. The meeting produced a list of tradable articles, but frozen Japanese funds and a possible American blacklist threatened the plan.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Japanese air travelers in Latin America
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports planned or completed flights by Tanaka, Kiyoshi Sakuma, and Yoshio Ishii.
subfiles.summary: The FBI relayed confidential information on three Japanese travelers moving between Havana, Mexico City, Panama City, Lima, and San Salvador in early September 1941. Copies were supplied to naval and military intelligence.

subfiles.title: FBI letter and list of Japanese air travel in Central America and Mexico
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits an August 29 list of Japanese nationals and their recent airline movements.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure records dated journeys between Mexico, Cristóbal, Panama, Tegucigalpa, San José, and Brownsville from June through August 1941. It identifies numerous travelers, including Hidenari Terasaki, Yoshio Ishii, Takeshi Hara, and Tsuneo Wachi.

subfiles.title: Naval District report of Japanese departures for Lima
subfiles.about: Reports two groups of Japanese passengers departing the Canal Zone for Lima.
subfiles.summary: The message states that Takachi, Nakatsuka, and Keizo Komiya were due to leave for Lima. It adds that Madgeta Roishii and Mohoya Simatcushita had already departed the Canal Zone for Lima by airplane.

subfiles.title: War Department radiogram on Hiramu Hata's journey
subfiles.to: War Department and distributed intelligence agencies
subfiles.about: Reports Hiramu Hata's departure from Balboa for Mexico and Manzanillo.
subfiles.summary: Hiramu Hata, head of the Nippon Trade Company in Panama City, left Balboa aboard a Pan American Airways flight. He was expected to continue from Mexico City to Manzanillo and board the Heiyo Maru.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Mexico concerning Hiramu Hata
subfiles.about: Notifies the embassy of Hiramu Hata's reported route to Manzanillo.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeated intelligence that Hata had left Balboa on September 12 for Mexico City. It stated that he intended to proceed to Manzanillo to board the vessel identified in the OCR as the Helve Maru.

subfiles.title: FBI letter and September 29 travel list
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides information about air reservations and movements by Japanese nationals and Margot Haase.
subfiles.summary: The letter reports travel involving Miami, Rio de Janeiro, New York, Auckland, and San Francisco, including the plans of German national Margot Haase. Its enclosure lists Hiramu Hata and a group of Japanese travelers moving through Brownsville and Mexico City, plus a reservation from Barranquilla to Miami.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on monitoring Nakamura's traveling group
subfiles.about: Recommends collecting file information and asking Mexico City about a repeatedly traveling Japanese group.
subfiles.summary: Toop considered Nakamura the most important member of the group listed on the attached travel sheet, although its exact activities were unclear. He proposed a file search and a request for reporting from the embassy in Mexico City.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Japanese intra-South American trade organization
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Describes an alleged Japanese trade network divided between Mitsui and Mitsubishi and lists its commodities and agents.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source said a Rio de Janeiro conference created a system for Japanese-controlled trade within South America, with Mitsui responsible for Panama through Mexico and Mitsubishi for South America. The report describes coded instructions from Tokyo and lists cement, coffee, oranges, textiles, pig iron, clay, and wax as proposed commodities. It names agents or offices in Uruguay, Chile, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting the Japanese trade report to Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Forwards the September 30 confidential report on Japanese inter-American commercial organization.
subfiles.summary: The Department sent the embassy a copy of a government-source report about Japanese inter-American commercial activity. The transmission was explicitly for the embassy's confidential information.

subfiles.title: Final page of Costa Rica Report No. 5872 on Japanese air travel
subfiles.about: Continues a dated list of Japanese travelers moving through Central America and Mexico.
subfiles.summary: This surviving final page lists movements from late July through August 25 involving Terasaki, Tsuji, Ishii, Hara, Wachi, and others. It is marked page eight and identifies E. Andino as the military attaché responsible for the report.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Sakuma, Ichimura, and Ishii
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports the travel and passport details of three Nippon Trading Company representatives.
subfiles.summary: Kiyoshi Sakuma, Matsujiro Ichimura, and Yoshio Ishii reportedly traveled from Cristóbal to Lima on June 22 and left Lima aboard the Heiyo Maru on September 6. The FBI supplied passport details and noted that Ishii had entered the United States at Seattle in 1934.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to circular on the Japanese Intelligence Service
subfiles.to: All American diplomatic officers in the other American republics
subfiles.about: Points to a circular summarizing reports on Japanese intelligence activities.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references the subject of the Japanese Intelligence Service to a circular dated October 16, 1941. The original was filed under 701.9411/1494a rather than reproduced here.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Terasaki's arrival in Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: References a report that Hidenari Terasaki arrived in Buenos Aires with Rokuro Shinohara.
subfiles.summary: The card records that Terasaki reached Buenos Aires on August 9 accompanied by Japanese diplomat Rokuro Shinohara. It directs researchers to despatch 3471 in file 701.9411/1515.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Terasaki's movements
subfiles.about: References a Peruvian report on Hidenari Terasaki's movements.
subfiles.summary: The card identifies a report from Peru concerning Terasaki's travel. It directs the reader to despatch 2156 in file 701.9411/1516.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Guatemala's response to Japanese intelligence information
subfiles.about: References a report that Guatemala's foreign minister appreciated information about Japanese intelligence activities.
subfiles.summary: The foreign minister reportedly expressed appreciation for the intelligence supplied to him. The sheet refers researchers to document 2246 in file 701.9411/1514.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Terasaki's activities and associates
subfiles.about: References Justice Department information on Hidenari Terasaki and his associates.
subfiles.summary: The card identifies Terasaki as First Secretary of the Japanese Embassy and notes that the underlying report concerns his activities and associations. The original was filed under 701.9411/1519.

subfiles.title: Naval intelligence report on alleged Japanese espionage headquarters and Axis plans
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence, using G-2 Panama Canal Department information
subfiles.about: Relays allegations about a San Diego espionage headquarters, Japanese-German cooperation, arms shipments, submarines, and plans in the Pacific.
subfiles.summary: A reportedly reliable source placed the headquarters of Japanese espionage in the Americas in a Japanese restaurant in San Diego and alleged an agent network throughout Mexico, Central America, and western South America. The report also claimed German-Japanese cooperation in supply bases and arms traffic, Japanese submarines intended for attacks on the Panama Canal, and negotiations to use Easter Island. It characterized Japanese policy as delaying American attention while preparing moves toward the Dutch East Indies and the Philippines.

subfiles.title: Coordinator of Information cover letter to Dean Acheson
subfiles.to: Dean G. Acheson, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards an enclosed survey of Japanese propaganda and espionage despite concern that it may have arrived too late.
subfiles.summary: The brief personal letter transmits an enclosure to Acheson. Its timing, two days after the Pearl Harbor attack, is acknowledged in the remark that the material may be too late.

subfiles.title: Japanese Propaganda and Espionage in North and South America
subfiles.from: Coordinator of Information, Central Information Division
subfiles.to: Dean G. Acheson and government intelligence users
subfiles.about: Summarizes COI files and lists people, businesses, officials, publications, and broadcasts possibly aiding Japanese propaganda, espionage, or trade.
subfiles.summary: The survey identifies major FBI, naval, military, financial-control, and diplomatic reports on Japanese activities in the United States and Latin America. It compiles names and organizations associated with favorable publicity, intelligence work, commercial dealings, bullion movements, strategic exports, and Axis collaboration in the United States, Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Costa Rica, Cuba, Ecuador, Mexico, and Peru. It also notes Japanese books and radio broadcasts directed at North America while cautioning that the files contained no single comprehensive list of propagandists or spies.

subfiles.title: Foreign Activity Correlation routing note requesting information
subfiles.about: Asks whether the division can supply information requested by Colonel Donovan's office.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten routing note forwards a request originating with the Coordinator of Information. It seeks assistance from the relevant State Department division in compiling the requested material.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum listing pro-Japanese propagandists
subfiles.to: Foreign Activity Correlation and Mr. Warren
subfiles.about: Names Americans and Canadians suspected of favorable propaganda or publicity work for Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum lists Carroll Lunt, Ralph Townsend, Harry Paxton Howard, Charles Bishop Kinney, George Gorman, and Frederick V. Williams. It adds persons said to have received South Manchurian Railway or Manchukuo grants and suggests examining architect Antonin Raymond's relations with the Japanese government.

subfiles.title: Coordinator of Information request for Japanese propaganda intelligence
subfiles.about: Requests information and names of Japanese propaganda agents in North and South America.
subfiles.summary: The requester asks for all available information on Japanese propaganda throughout the Americas. Particular interest is expressed in American or European agents working for Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William Donovan
subfiles.from: George A. Gordon, Department of State
subfiles.to: Colonel William J. Donovan, Coordinator of Information
subfiles.about: Responds to Donovan's request by forwarding lists of suspected espionage associates and Japanese government agents.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Donovan's November 17 memorandum concerning Japanese propaganda and agents. Gordon encloses one list of persons believed to have engaged in espionage and another of past or present agents, while warning that it was not known whether every listed agent had participated in espionage.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: persons associated with Japanese espionage activities
subfiles.about: Lists persons reportedly associated with espionage or traveling in the Americas in Japan's interests.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure begins with Hidenari Terasaki and several news representatives, lawyers, and other contacts reportedly connected with Japanese intelligence. It then names a traveling group of Japanese nationals and repeats the list of American and Canadian figures suspected of favorable propaganda or publicity work.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: former and present agents of the Japanese government
subfiles.about: Lists individuals and organizations under official investigation as former or present Japanese government agents.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure presents a long roster of people, companies, chambers of commerce, shipping lines, cultural bodies, advertising firms, and information agencies. It describes them as subjects of another government department's investigation without asserting that all had conducted espionage.

subfiles.title: Rio de Janeiro telegram on increased Japanese coded traffic to Lima
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports a sudden burst of approximately thirty Japanese government-code messages routed through La Paz to Lima.
subfiles.summary: Radio monitors observed about thirty messages from Tokyo on the night of December 10, compared with a previous average of roughly one per week. Messages from Tokyo bore Togo's signature and were relayed from La Paz to Lima under the signature Iriyerbo.

subfiles.title: Departmental transmittal of the Rio coded-traffic report
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the December 11 Rio de Janeiro report on coded Japanese traffic.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwarded the information to military, naval, and federal investigators in the hope that it would prove useful. The attached item was identified as a paraphrase of confidential telegram 1995 from Rio de Janeiro.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of telegram 1995 from Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Restates the report of approximately thirty coded Japanese messages routed to Lima.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase records an exceptional increase in radio messages from Tokyo to La Paz for relay to Lima. It preserves the signatures Togo and Iriyerbo while omitting the original cable's formatting.

subfiles.title: Internal warning concerning coded traffic to Peru and Chile
subfiles.about: Interprets heavy message traffic to Lima and Santiago as a possible warning of German-Japanese action on South America's west coast.
subfiles.summary: Toop compared the La Paz–Lima traffic with Japanese and German messages routed to Santiago and cited evidence of Axis intelligence cooperation. He suggested discreetly warning Chile and Peru and speculated about sabotage raids or an Axis naval demonstration intended to distract the United States. The memorandum explicitly presented these scenarios as informed guesses rather than confirmed plans.

subfiles.title: Urgent warning telegram to Santiago
subfiles.about: Warns Chile of increased Japanese and German coded traffic and requests heightened vigilance.
subfiles.summary: The Department summarized the messages routed to Lima and the Japanese- and German-code traffic sent to Santiago on December 11. It advised that the increase and changed routing could indicate activity by Axis elements and asked the embassy to alert appropriate Chilean authorities under existing commitments.

subfiles.title: Urgent inquiry to Buenos Aires about coded-message routing
subfiles.about: Describes abnormal coded traffic and asks Buenos Aires to consider the significance of its routing.
subfiles.summary: The telegram recounts the Tokyo–La Paz–Lima traffic and the relay of Japanese messages through Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires to Santiago. It notes that radio-technical considerations did not explain the differing routes and links the issue to unusually heavy German-code traffic to Santiago. Lima and Santiago were also informed.

subfiles.title: Rio telegram on coded traffic to Santiago
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports intercepted Japanese- and German-government-code messages destined for Santiago.
subfiles.summary: Rio's monitors intercepted many Japanese government-code messages relayed from Tokyo through Rio de Janeiro and Buenos Aires to Santiago. They also detected an unusual number of German government-code messages from Rio and Buenos Aires for the same destination.

subfiles.title: Japanese fishing vessel apprehended at Santos
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports the detention of a Japanese fishing vessel carrying homemade bombs at Santos.
subfiles.summary: The embassy's naval attaché reported that maritime police at Santos apprehended the vessel the previous day. Homemade bombs were allegedly found aboard.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution of the Santos vessel report
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the Rio despatch concerning a Japanese fishing vessel at Santos.
subfiles.summary: The Department sent copies of the December 12 despatch to the three principal domestic intelligence bodies. The enclosure was identified by title and as strictly confidential.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires report on alleged Japanese suicide corps and commodity purchases
subfiles.about: Relays claims of Japanese suicide sabotage corps in the Americas and secret Argentine purchasing by Taguchi and Hara.
subfiles.summary: A usually reliable source alleged that Japanese residents in the United States and other American republics had organized suicide corps for sabotage. The same source described a Japanese “suicide army” of fliers and submarine crews and said Taguchi and Hara were covertly buying Argentine products for shipment to Japan. The allegations were reported as source information rather than independently verified facts.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution of the Buenos Aires suicide-corps report
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the Buenos Aires report on alleged Japanese sabotage organizations.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwarded a true copy of the original report to military, naval, and federal intelligence agencies. The memorandum itself adds no new substantive intelligence.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Ecuadorian propaganda publication to the Library of Congress
subfiles.about: Forwards a propaganda publication received with a Quito legation despatch.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary continued the Department's practice of supplying the Library of Congress with propaganda issued in other American republics. The enclosed publication had accompanied Quito despatch 2395 of December 19, 1941.

subfiles.title: Research and Publication routing memorandum on propaganda pamphlets
subfiles.about: Requests return of unneeded propaganda pamphlets so they can be sent to the Library of Congress.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that Welles and Berle had instructed the division to help the Library acquire foreign propaganda. It notes that the Library was coordinating with the Coordinator of Information in using such material.

subfiles.title: Quito despatch on Japanese propaganda distributed after Pearl Harbor
subfiles.about: Reports Naguno's distribution of Japanese propaganda and encloses two pro-Japanese Spanish-language publications.
subfiles.summary: Long reported that Naguno was spreading propaganda in Quito about twenty-four hours after the attack on American forces, including to a foreign-office employee. He described the Buenos Aires magazine Oriente y Occidente and Francisco Javier Díaz's Chilean pamphlet on war between the United States and Japan. The minister concluded that Japanese propaganda machinery had been prepared before the December 7 attack.

subfiles.title: Internal comment on proposed propaganda inquiry
subfiles.about: Defends seeking current evidence of Japanese propaganda despite prewar legal prohibitions.
subfiles.summary: The writer agrees that desk review of circular telegrams would be desirable but identifies time as the chief obstacle. The memorandum argues that Ambassador Wilson's earlier reports on legal bans did not show what Japanese actors were doing after war began and notes that formal prohibitions did not always stop propaganda.

subfiles.title: Circular inquiry on current Japanese propaganda
subfiles.to: Chiefs of mission in the other American republics except Brazil
subfiles.about: Requests reports on Japanese propaganda and recommendations for American countermeasures.
subfiles.summary: The Department asked each mission to cable the nature and effect of Japanese propaganda then being disseminated. Missions were also asked what measures the United States should adopt or intensify.

subfiles.title: Port-au-Prince reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports no Japanese business representatives or propaganda in Haiti.
subfiles.summary: The mission stated that no known Japanese business representatives remained locally. It also knew of no Japanese propaganda in circulation.

subfiles.title: Caracas reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Frank P. Corrigan, American Embassy, Caracas
subfiles.about: Reports limited prewar Japanese news broadcasting and no known continuing propaganda in Venezuela.
subfiles.summary: One local radio station had reportedly broadcast Domei material before December 7 alongside Havas, Stefani, and British-supplied news. After the British legation approached the station owner, the practice stopped, and the embassy knew of no other Japanese propaganda dissemination.

subfiles.title: Santiago reply on Japanese propaganda and Chilean vulnerability
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, American Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese propaganda as limited but warns that fear of Japanese attack was influencing Chilean policy.
subfiles.summary: Bowers said visible Japanese propaganda was modest, although Chilean journalists hosted by Japan had supplied some favorable stories. He emphasized a widespread Chilean belief that Japan could attack coastal commerce and that the United States could not yet protect the coast, encouraging caution toward Tokyo. He recommended credible publicity emphasizing Japan's eventual military and economic weakness.

subfiles.title: La Paz reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, American mission, La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports no active Japanese propaganda in Bolivia but notes the psychological effect of Japanese victories.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese colony was described as disorganized by disrupted commerce and the temporary absence of the chargé d'affaires. Dawson nevertheless believed Japanese military successes in the Far East were affecting Bolivian attitudes toward the war.

subfiles.title: Ciudad Trujillo reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Robert M. Scotten, American mission, Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.about: Reports no pro-Japanese propaganda in the Dominican Republic.
subfiles.summary: The mission found no evidence of propaganda favorable to Japan. It added that the country's only Japanese subject was confined in a concentration camp.

subfiles.title: San Salvador reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports no Japanese propaganda and strict surveillance of Japanese residents in El Salvador.
subfiles.summary: The mission emphatically stated that no Japanese propaganda was being conducted. All eight Japanese men and women resident in the country were under strict surveillance.

subfiles.title: San José reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Arthur Bliss Lane, American Legation, San José
subfiles.about: Reports that no Japanese propaganda had come to the legation's attention in Costa Rica.
subfiles.summary: The response is brief and categorical. The legation had observed no Japanese propaganda in Costa Rica.

subfiles.title: Asunción reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports no discoverable Japanese propaganda or similar activity in Paraguay.
subfiles.summary: Frost stated that he had been unable to learn of any Japanese propaganda locally. No comparable Japanese activity was identified.

subfiles.title: Bogotá reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports very little Japanese propaganda in Colombia, apart from distorted press despatches.
subfiles.summary: The embassy judged Japanese propaganda slight and without visible effect. It noted distorted Tokyo reports routed through Vichy by United Press and Havas and printed only by El Siglo.

subfiles.title: Panama reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Edwin C. Wilson, American Embassy, Panama
subfiles.about: Reports no Japanese propaganda following Panama's prohibition of anti-democratic propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Wilson stated that Japanese propaganda was absent in Panama. He attributed the situation to a November 21 decree prohibiting all anti-democratic propaganda.

subfiles.title: Mexico reply on Japanese propaganda and countermeasures
subfiles.about: Describes rumor-spreading and German-funded pro-Japanese publicity and recommends press and radio countermeasures.
subfiles.summary: The embassy characterized Japanese propaganda as small in volume and spread mainly through Japanese residents, Mexican contacts, and newspapers subsidized with German funds. It endorsed Coordination Committee projects for press publicity and long-wave news broadcasting, including a proposed monthly press expenditure.

subfiles.title: Lima reply on Axis propaganda and recommended American response
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Describes word-of-mouth Axis propaganda in Peru and proposes stronger, sustained American radio and economic messaging.
subfiles.summary: Norweb reported rumors promoted by Japanese military attachés about Japanese victories, the American fleet, convoy service, and purchases of Peruvian materials with gold. He believed the campaign had limited effect on influential opinion but may have encouraged some officials toward neutrality. He recommended better editing of Tokyo-derived wire reports, repeated emphasis on American military and economic strength, and stronger sixteen-hour daily broadcasts to South America.

subfiles.title: Tegucigalpa reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: John D. Erwin, American mission, Tegucigalpa
subfiles.about: Reports little Japanese propaganda in Honduras beyond occasional free radio news used by a local newspaper.
subfiles.summary: The mission found no appreciable Japanese propaganda and no conspicuous cases of outright advocacy. One newspaper had occasionally used official Japanese radio news when authentic paid news service was unavailable.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires reply on Japanese propaganda in Argentina
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, American Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese propaganda channels in Argentina and identifies Albino Pugnalin as the principal local agent.
subfiles.summary: Armour listed Japanese-language newspapers, Berlin and Tokyo news services, Oriente y Occidente, cultural groups, a tourist bureau, pamphlets, films, and lectures as propaganda channels. He said the effort increasingly coordinated with German propaganda but remained limited in effect. The embassy asked the Foreign Office to prevent a proposed Pugnalin article opposing Argentine-American cooperation and recommended clearer presentation of the American position.

subfiles.title: Guatemala reply on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese propaganda reached Guatemala chiefly through wire services and weak shortwave broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: The mission identified United Press, Associated Press, and Japanese, German, and Italian shortwave radio as the only channels carrying such material. Few Guatemalans were thought to listen to Japanese broadcasts, whose poor reception and Spanish reportedly produced an unfavorable impression. Page 327 duplicates the telegram text on page 326.
